title: 1 Chronicles 21:1–8
context: The Chronicler retells the census of 2 Samuel 24. Where 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD’s anger burned against Israel and he moved David, 1 Chronicles 21:1 says Satan stood up against Israel and moved David. As in the 2 Samuel 24 notes, both traditions hold the two accounts together and place the guilt on David; the question of how God’s agency relates to evil agents is treated in the key contrast at Judges 9:23. The account also differs from Samuel in the census figures (21:5; compare 2 Samuel 24:9) and adds that Levi and Benjamin were not counted (21:6). These differences are named here, not harmonized.

verses.text: Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to take a census of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Satan stood up against Israel and moved David to take a census. In line with the 2 Samuel 24:1 notes, Arminian readers see God permitting Satan’s agency in judicial anger, so that David is given over to a desire already present in him (James 1:13). The Judges 9:23 box treats this question.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hold 2 Samuel 24:1 and this verse together: God governs all events, including Satan’s activity, so Chronicles names the secondary agent and Samuel the sovereign one (Job 1–2). Both traditions deny that God is the author of sin. Some take the word as an adversary rather than a name.

verses.text: David said to Joab and to the princes of the people, “Go, count Israel from Beersheba even to Dan; and bring me word, that I may know how many there are.”
verses.arminianNotes: David tells Joab and the princes to count Israel from Beersheba to Dan. Arminian readers observe that the reason given, that I may know how many there are, hints at a king measuring his security by numbers rather than by trust in God (Psalm 20:7).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the order of the boundaries is reversed from Samuel’s Dan to Beersheba, a small difference of wording. The motive is left unstated in both books, and many interpreters treat the precise sin as a matter of discussion rather than certainty.

verses.text: Joab said, “May the LORD make his people a hundred times as many as they are. But, my lord the king, aren’t they all my lord’s servants? Why does my lord require this thing? Why will he be a cause of guilt to Israel?”
verses.arminianNotes: Joab protests that all the people already belong to the king and asks why David would be a cause of guilt to Israel. Arminian readers see a warning offered and refused, one of several moments when David could have stopped before acting.
verses.reformedNotes: Joab’s question about guilt has no counterpart in 2 Samuel 24:3. Reformed readers note that Joab, hardly a model of piety elsewhere, still saw that a king’s sin would fall on his people, a theme that runs through the rest of the chapter.

verses.text: Nevertheless the king’s word prevailed against Joab. Therefore Joab departed and went throughout all Israel, then came to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The king’s word prevailed against Joab. Arminian readers stress that David chose to override wise counsel, and they see a lesson for leaders who silence the people best placed to warn them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Chronicles compresses the census journey into a single line, while 2 Samuel 24:5-8 traces Joab’s route in detail. The narrative assigns the decision clearly to David, consistent with the guilt placed on him in Samuel.

verses.text: Joab gave the sum of the census of the people to David. All those of Israel were one million one hundred thousand men who drew a sword; and in Judah were four hundred seventy thousand men who drew a sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Joab reports one million one hundred thousand men in Israel and four hundred seventy thousand in Judah. Arminian readers note that 2 Samuel 24:9 gives eight hundred thousand and five hundred thousand, and they leave the difference as it stands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise name the difference from 2 Samuel 24:9 without forcing a harmonization. Interpreters have offered several explanations for these figures, and none is settled; what both accounts share is a count of men who drew the sword, a measure of military strength.

verses.text: But he didn’t count Levi and Benjamin among them, for the king’s word was abominable to Joab.
verses.arminianNotes: Joab did not count Levi and Benjamin because the king’s word was abominable to him. Arminian readers see Joab’s partial resistance as conscience at work, even in a hard man, and note that this detail has no parallel in 2 Samuel 24.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Levi was set apart from military censuses in the law (Numbers 1:47-49). Why Benjamin was also left out is not explained, and interpreters differ on the reason; the verse simply records the omission and Joab’s disgust.

verses.text: God was displeased with this thing; therefore he struck Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: God was displeased and struck Israel. Arminian readers note that Chronicles mentions God’s displeasure before David’s confession, while 2 Samuel 24:10 begins with David’s heart striking him; they read divine displeasure as a call to awaken the king’s conscience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s displeasure as holy and just, falling on the nation because of its king’s sin. The order of events differs from Samuel’s account, and the Chronicler’s placement underlines that the census itself offended God.

verses.text: David said to God, “I have sinned greatly, in that I have done this thing. But now put away, I beg you, the iniquity of your servant, for I have done very foolishly.”
verses.arminianNotes: David confesses, I have sinned greatly, and asks God to put away his iniquity. Arminian readers see genuine repentance freely offered in response to conviction, and they note that David names his act as very foolish rather than excusing it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see confession as the fruit of God’s work in the heart, and they note the close match with 2 Samuel 24:10. David takes the guilt on himself, consistent with the Samuel notes, and asks for forgiveness, not merely relief.
